questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three functions whose optional values sit in the signature as defaults.

How this works in Python

Java has no default parameter values. When you want a short call and a long call, you write the method twice and let the short one delegate.

String describe(String valveId) {
    return describe(valveId, 3.5);
}

String describe(String valveId, double pressureKpa) {
    return valveId + " at " + pressureKpa + " kPa";
}

Two signatures, one behaviour, and the constant 3.5 buried in a method body where no caller can see it. Add a timeout and you write a third overload. Python replaces the whole set with one def.

def describe(valve_id: str, pressure_kpa: float = 3.5) -> str:
    return f"{valve_id} at {pressure_kpa} kPa"

= 3.5 in the parameter list makes pressure_kpa a default parameter. A caller who omits it gets 3.5. A caller who supplies it gets what they supplied. The value now sits in the signature, so it reaches the reader, the documentation and the editor's hint rather than hiding in a body.

One ordering rule comes with it. Every parameter carrying a default has to sit after every parameter without one, because Python fills the positional slots from the left. Break that and the def line itself is refused with SyntaxError.

Now the call site. Java matches arguments by position and by nothing else. Python lets a caller pass an argument by name.

reading("V1", timeout_s=5)

An argument passed by name is a keyword argument. An argument matched by position alone is a positional argument, and Java has only the second kind. The keyword form sends 5 to the parameter called timeout_s whatever position that parameter sits in, so the call above skips straight over pressure_kpa and leaves it on its default. Java cannot skip a middle argument at all, and its answer is another overload.

Name every argument and the order stops mattering.

reading(timeout_s=1, valve_id="V3", pressure_kpa=2.0)

Two limits apply. Keyword arguments have to come after positional ones in a call, and the parser refuses anything else. A parameter already filled by position may not then be filled by name, and that one raises TypeError: reading() got multiple values for argument 'valve_id'. Read the message as the interpreter telling you the same slot was filled twice.

One more fact about the default, and it carries further than it looks. Python works the default value out once, at the moment the def statement runs, and stores it on the function object. Read describe.__defaults__ and you find it sitting there as (3.5,).

A name wrapped in double underscores is called a dunder, short for double underscore. It marks a name the language owns. __defaults__ is one of them, and it holds a tuple of every default the function was born with.

Java's short overload behaves the other way round. Its body runs on every call, so its 3.5 is produced afresh each time. The Python default is produced once and handed out forever. For a number that difference costs you nothing. For a value that can be changed in place it costs you a great deal, and that is the whole of the next tier.

One convention about spacing. Without an annotation you write timeout_s=30 with no spaces at all. With an annotation you write timeout_s: int = 30 with spaces round the equals sign. Every Python reader expects both forms in their place.

Your task

STANDARD_KPA already sits in the answer box. Use it as the default rather than typing the number twice.

  • describe(valve_id: str, pressure_kpa: float = STANDARD_KPA) -> str returns V1 at 3.5 kPa for the valve V1 at the standard pressure.
  • reading(valve_id: str, pressure_kpa: float = STANDARD_KPA, timeout_s: int = 30) -> str returns the three values separated by single spaces, so V1 3.5 30.
  • quick_check(valve_id: str) -> str calls reading with a timeout of five seconds and returns what comes back. It leaves the pressure alone, which means naming the argument it does set and mentioning the pressure nowhere.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write one def per name. A second def under the same name is not an overload, it is a rebinding, and the first one is gone.
  • Put the default in the signature. No if in a body to patch up a missing argument.
  • Let quick_check skip the pressure by naming the timeout. Neither 3.5 nor STANDARD_KPA appears anywhere inside it.
  • Annotate every parameter and every return, with spaces round the equals sign wherever a parameter carries both an annotation and a default.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

expected.text: V1 at 3.5 kPa V2 at 7.0 kPa (3.5,)

testcode.text: print(reading("V1")) print(reading("V1", timeout_s=5)) print(reading(timeout_s=1, valve_id="V3", pressure_kpa=2.0)) print(quick_check("V4")) print(reading.__defaults__)

expected.text: reading() missing 1 required positional argument: 'valve_id' reading() got multiple values for argument 'valve_id' reading() takes from 1 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given reading() got an unexpected keyword argument 'mode'

import ast import inspect import pathlib import re
# Parse the file rather than scanning its text. CodeRunner stores a second copy # of the answer in a string, and a text scan would count that copy too. tree = ast.parse(pathlib.Path(inspect.getsourcefile(describe)).read_text()) written = inspect.getsource(describe) + inspect.getsource(reading) call = inspect.getsource(quick_check) for label in ("describe", "reading", "quick_check"): defs = [n for n in tree.body if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef) and n.name == label] assert len(defs) == 1, "rule broken: one def per name" assert not re.search(r"\bif\b", written), "rule broken: put the default in the signature" assert describe.__defaults__ == (3.5,), "rule broken: the default belongs in the signature" assert reading.__defaults__ == (3.5, 30), "rule broken: both defaults belong in the signature" assert "timeout_s=" in call, "rule broken: name the argument you are setting" assert "STANDARD_KPA" not in call, "rule broken: quick_check leaves the pressure alone" for name in ("valve_id", "pressure_kpa", "timeout_s", "return"): assert name in reading.__annotations__, "rule broken: annotate every parameter and the return" for name in ("valve_id", "return"): assert name in describe.__annotations__, "rule broken: annotate every parameter and the return" assert name in quick_check.__annotations__, "rule broken: annotate every parameter and the return"
print(quick_check("V9")) print(describe("V9"), reading("V9")) print(sorted(reading.__annotations__)) print(describe(pressure_kpa=0.0, valve_id="V0"))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write two repaired functions whose defaults are built fresh on every call.

How this works in Python

Java has no default parameter values. When you want a short call and a long call, you write two methods and let the short one delegate.

void record(String event) {
    record(event, new ArrayList<>());
}

void record(String event, List<String> journal) {
    journal.add(event);
}

Python writes one def and puts the value straight into the signature.

def record(event, journal=[]):
    journal.append(event)
    return journal

Read that as the Java pair above and you read it wrong. new ArrayList<>() runs on every call to the short overload. The [] runs exactly once, at the moment the def statement itself executes.

Python builds that empty list once and stores it on the function object. A function is an object here, and every object carries attributes. An attribute is a named value living on an object, the way a field lives on a Java instance. record.__defaults__ is one such attribute. It holds a tuple of every default value the function was born with, and the list is in it.

A name wrapped in double underscores is called a dunder, short for double underscore. It marks a name the language owns.

So every call that omits journal appends to the same list, and that list lives as long as the process does. It reads like a local variable. It behaves like a static field.

The repair is the None sentinel from the dictionaries topic. None is Python's null, and a sentinel is a value you park in a slot to mean "the caller gave me nothing".

def record(event: str, journal: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    if journal is None:
        journal = []
    journal.append(event)
    return journal

None is immutable, so freezing it costs you nothing. The fresh list now gets built in the body, and the body runs on every call. Read list[str] | None as "a list of strings or nothing at all", which is the honest description of a parameter carrying a sentinel.

Write is None here, never if not journal. The truthiness topic showed you that an empty list is falsey, which means Python reads it as false in a condition. A caller who hands you an empty list wants that list appended to. if not journal would throw it away and hand back a different one.

The trap is wider than lists. Any expression in a default is frozen when the def line runs. Name a module-level variable in a default and you capture the value it held at import time. A module-level name is bound at the top of the file, outside every function. It is the closest thing Python has to a static field. Rebind that name later and the default does not notice.

Your task

Three things already sit in the answer box. SHIFT is a module-level string. broken_record and broken_label carry the bug. Leave all three exactly as they are, because the tests put the bug on screen before they put the fix on screen.

  • record(event: str, journal: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str] appends event to journal and returns it. Two calls that omit journal never see each other's data. A caller who supplies a list gets that same list object back with the event appended.
  • label(event: str, shift: str | None = None) -> str returns night: handover for the event handover under the shift night. When the caller omits shift, read the value SHIFT holds right now rather than a copy frozen at import time.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Never put a mutable literal in a parameter list again, for the rest of this course. = [], = {} and = set() are all banned.
  • Fix it with is None. if not journal is banned, because it also fires on a caller's legitimately empty list.
  • Do not dodge the trap with a global, a class attribute or functools. One sentinel and one line.
  • Leave broken_record and broken_label untouched. The bug goes on screen before the fix does.
  • Annotate both signatures you write, parameters and return alike. A sentinel parameter is list[str] | None, never bare list[str], and never Optional.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: print(broken_record("pump trip")) print(broken_record("valve stuck")) print(broken_record("pump trip")) print(broken_record.__defaults__)

expected.text: ['pump trip'] ['pump trip', 'valve stuck'] ['pump trip', 'valve stuck', 'pump trip'] (['pump trip', 'valve stuck', 'pump trip'],)

testcode.text: print(record("pump trip")) print(record("valve stuck")) mine = ["earlier"] print(record("relay fault", mine)) print(mine) print(record.__defaults__)
SHIFT = "day" print(broken_label("handover")) print(broken_label.__defaults__) print(label("handover")) print(label("handover", "swing")) print(label.__defaults__)

expected.text: night: handover ('night',) day: handover swing: handover (None,)

import inspect import re
fixed = inspect.getsource(record) + inspect.getsource(label) assert "is None" in fixed, "rule broken: fix it with is None" assert not re.search(r"if\s+not\s+journal", fixed), "rule broken: use is None, not falsiness" assert not re.search(r"\bglobal\b", fixed), "rule broken: no global" assert "functools" not in fixed, "rule broken: no functools trickery" assert not re.search(r"\bclass\b", fixed), "rule broken: no class attribute" for fn in (record, label): assert fn.__defaults__ == (None,), "rule broken: the only default is the None sentinel" assert isinstance(broken_record.__defaults__[0], list), "leave broken_record exactly as it is"
empty = [] print(record("solo", empty) is empty) print(record("a"), record("b")) print(label("x"))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write one function with positional-only and keyword-only parameters, plus a wrapper that passes everything through.

How this works in Python

Java gives you one name and many signatures. The compiler picks the method by the argument types.

void openValve(String id) { ... }
void openValve(String id, double kPa) { ... }
void openValve(String id, double kPa, int timeoutS) { ... }

Python has no overloading at all. A def statement binds a name, the same way x = 5 binds a name. Write def open_valve three times and the third binding wins. The first two are gone, and nothing warns you.

One Python signature carries the work of the whole overload set, and of the Builder pattern, and of the Map<String, Object> options bag. Start with one idea Java does not have.

A Python caller may pass an argument by name. open_valve("V1", timeout_s=5) sends 5 to the parameter called timeout_s, whatever position that parameter sits in. An argument passed by name is a keyword argument. An argument matched by position alone is a positional argument. Java has only the second kind.

Four pieces of grammar build on that.

*args collects any leftover positional arguments into a tuple. It is Java varargs with no type and no last-parameter restriction.

**kwargs collects any leftover keyword arguments into a dict. Java has nothing like it. The names arrive as keys and the values arrive as values, and you read the result with everything you learned in the dictionaries topic.

A bare * in the parameter list is a wall. Every parameter after it is keyword-only, so a caller must name it. No argument can slide into the wrong slot by sitting in the wrong position.

A / in the parameter list is the opposite wall. Every parameter before it is positional-only, so a caller may not name it. The identifier belongs to you, and renaming it later breaks nobody.

def open_valve(valve_id, /, *, pressure_kpa, timeout_s=30, **audit):
    ...

Call it with open_valve("V1", pressure_kpa=3.5, operator="rangi"). The first argument fills valve_id by position, and pressure_kpa arrives by name. timeout_s falls back to 30.

operator matches no parameter at all, so **audit collects it as {'operator': 'rangi'}.

The same two stars work at the call site, where they spread instead of collect. f(*items) unpacks a tuple into positional arguments. f(**options) unpacks a dict into keyword arguments. That gives you a pass-through wrapper that names no parameter at all.

def forward(*args: object, **kwargs: object) -> str:
    return open_valve(*args, **kwargs)

Now the annotations. The type hints topic told you that an annotation looks like a Java type declaration and that nothing at run time checks it. This exercise is where you watch that hold.

The interpreter evaluates each annotation, stores the results in the __annotations__ dict on the function object, and then ignores them forever. Pass a str where you annotated float and the call succeeds. There is no compiler here, and there are no checked exceptions.

An annotation on a star parameter describes one collected item rather than the whole collection, so **audit: str says every audit value is a string, not that audit is one.

One test call breaks a wall on purpose. open_valve(valve_id="V1", pressure_kpa=3.5) passes valve_id by name. valve_id sits before the /, so it is positional-only and that name matches no parameter.

The name is not thrown away though. **audit collects it as an audit field, the positional slot stays empty, and the error reads missing 1 required positional argument. Read that message as proof that the wall held.

Your task

Three legacy_valve definitions already sit in the answer box. Leave them alone. They exist so the first test can prove that only the last one survived.

def open_valve(valve_id, /, *, pressure_kpa, timeout_s=30, **audit):
    ...
  • open_valve with exactly the signature shown above, plus an annotation on every parameter and on the return. Annotate valve_id as str, pressure_kpa as float, timeout_s as int, audit as str and the return as str. Return this exact string. 
    f"{valve_id} to {pressure_kpa} kPa over {timeout_s}s {audit}"
  • forward(*args: object, **kwargs: object) -> str, which calls open_valve and returns its result. forward must not mention a single one of open_valve's parameter names.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write exactly one def for open_valve. Do not dispatch on len(args) or isinstance, which is an overload table written by hand.
  • Put every safety-relevant parameter after a bare *, so no call site can slide an argument into the wrong slot. Put the identifier before a /, so no call site can rename it.
  • Collect the audit fields with **. A plain dict parameter is a different contract.
  • Annotate every parameter and the return, then read __annotations__ and watch the annotations stop nothing.
  • Let forward name none of open_valve's parameters. Two stars in, two stars out.
  • Annotate forward as well. Anything at all may pass through it, so its star parameters take object rather than Any, and it still returns str.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

expected.text: 3 legacy_valve() missing 2 required positional arguments: 'pressure_kpa' and 'timeout_s' three args: V1 3.5 10

testcode.text: print(open_valve("V1", pressure_kpa=3.5)) print(open_valve("V2", pressure_kpa=7.0, timeout_s=5, operator="rangi", ticket="T-88")) call = ("V3",) opts = {"pressure_kpa": 1.25, "site": "kaitaia"} print(forward(*call, **opts))

import inspect
src = inspect.getsource(open_valve) wrapper = inspect.getsource(forward) kinds = {name: str(p.kind) for name, p in inspect.signature(open_valve).parameters.items()} assert src.count("def open_valve") == 1, "rule broken: exactly one def for open_valve" assert kinds["valve_id"] == "POSITIONAL_ONLY", "rule broken: valve_id sits before a /" assert kinds["pressure_kpa"] == "KEYWORD_ONLY", "rule broken: pressure_kpa sits after a bare *" assert kinds["timeout_s"] == "KEYWORD_ONLY", "rule broken: timeout_s sits after a bare *" assert kinds["audit"] == "VAR_KEYWORD", "rule broken: collect the audit fields with **" assert "isinstance" not in src and "len(args)" not in src, "rule broken: no hand-written dispatch" for name in ("valve_id", "pressure_kpa", "timeout_s", "audit"): assert name in open_valve.__annotations__, "rule broken: annotate every parameter" assert name not in wrapper, "rule broken: forward must not name a parameter" assert "return" in open_valve.__annotations__, "rule broken: annotate the return"
print(list(kinds.values())) print(open_valve.__annotations__["pressure_kpa"].__name__) print(forward("V5", pressure_kpa=2.5, timeout_s=1))
